name: Cylindrical Waves and a Cosmic String
description: Outside a straight cosmic string, cylindrical gravitational waves form a vacuum geometry whose angle deficit is larger far from the axis.
convention: The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: For a circle around a positive tension cosmic string, the ratio of circumference to proper radius approaches a value below $2\pi$ as the radius tends to zero. The missing angle marks the string on the axis [gurtug_sakalli2003]. Cylindrical gravitational waves surround the string in a vacuum geometry [gurtug_sakalli2003, xanthopoulos1986cylindrical].¶In cylindrical coordinates $(t,\rho,\phi,z)$ and units of a length $\ell$, the line element is $ds^2/\ell^2=A(-dt^2+d\rho^2)+\rho^2X\,d\phi^2/Y+(Y/X)(dz-\omega\,d\phi)^2$ [gurtug_sakalli2003]. Here $A=\alpha^2X/(\tau^2+\sigma^2)$, $X=(1-p\tau)^2+q^2\sigma^2$, and $Y=X-2(1-p\tau)$. The twist is $\omega=2q(\sigma^2-1)(1-p\tau)/(pY)$, with $q^2-p^2=1$. The auxiliary coordinates obey $t=\tau\sigma$ and $\rho^2=(1+\tau^2)(\sigma^2-1)$.¶At the axis the deficit is $2\pi(1-1/|\alpha p|)$ [gurtug_sakalli2003]. It vanishes when $|\alpha p|=1$, leaving a regular axis. Far from the axis at fixed time, the corresponding deficit is $2\pi(1-1/|\alpha q|)$ [gurtug_sakalli2003]. At fixed $t$ and $\rho$, the limit $p\to\infty$ with $\alpha p=k>1$ approaches the locally flat exterior of a straight string [gurtug_sakalli2003]. Scaling time and radius by $k$ gives the angular term $R^2d\phi^2/k^2$, with $R=k\rho$.¶Basilis C. Xanthopoulos obtained this solution in 1986 through a complex transformation of the Kerr metric [xanthopoulos1986rotating]. The family is of Petrov type D and has no curvature singularities [gurtug_sakalli2003, xanthopoulos1986cylindrical]. Xanthopoulos described the waves as nonradiating [xanthopoulos1986cylindrical, garriga_verdaguer1987].¶Xanthopoulos coupled the waves to an electromagnetic field in 1987 [xanthopoulos1987em]. The electromagnetic families are of Petrov type D and include strings with an angle deficit on the axis [xanthopoulos1987em]. Athanasios Economou and Dimitri Tsoubelis found a broader family of cylindrical soliton waves in 1988, with the original vacuum geometry as a subfamily [economou_tsoubelis1988, kleidis2010]. Ulrich Sperhake and coauthors used the exact profiles of both polarizations to check numerical evolution in 2000 [sjodin2000dynamic, sperhake2000dynamic]. They reproduced those profiles with Cauchy-characteristic matching and a fully characteristic scheme, including null infinity in the numerical grid [sjodin2000dynamic, sperhake2000dynamic].¶Özay Gürtuğ and İzzet Sakallı added a massless scalar field in 2003 [gurtug_sakalli2003]. The scalar wave changes the angle deficit near the axis [gurtug_sakalli2003]. The scalar field tends to zero far from the string, leaving the asymptotic deficit unchanged [gurtug_sakalli2003]. With the scalar field present, the geometry is of Petrov type I [gurtug_sakalli2003].¶Xanthopoulos had interpreted the axis as a rotating cosmic string [xanthopoulos1986rotating]. Jiří Bičák, Joseph Katz, and Donald Lynden-Bell evaluated the Komar angular momentum in 2008 and found it zero for this geometry [bicak_katz_lyndenbell2008]. The cross term in the line element couples the angular and longitudinal directions [gurtug_sakalli2003].¶Kostas Kleidis and coauthors added a Kerr-NUT parameter to an Einstein-Maxwell family in 2010 [kleidis2010]. The original vacuum geometry is its limit with no electromagnetic field and a vanishing Kerr-NUT parameter [kleidis2010]. At null infinity, the waves carry a nonzero C-energy flux, concentrated around the null directions [kleidis2010]. At fixed time, the flux tends to zero far from the axis [gurtug_sakalli2003]. Henrique P. de Oliveira and coauthors used this geometry to test a spectral method with separate radial domains in 2019 [barreto2019cylindrical]. Dividing the grid into two domains resolved the steep radial profiles of both polarizations more accurately [barreto2019cylindrical].

coordinates.convention: We use dimensionless coordinates $(\tau,\sigma,\phi,z)$, with $\sigma>1$ outside the axis. The cylindrical coordinates $t=\tau\sigma$ and $\rho^2=(1+\tau^2)(\sigma^2-1)$ have $t\in(-\infty,\infty)$ and $\rho>0$. The inverse is $\sigma=\sqrt{(D+1+\rho^2-t^2)/2}$ and $\tau=t/\sigma$, where $D=\sqrt{(1+\rho^2-t^2)^2+4t^2}$. A dot denotes differentiation with respect to an affine parameter.

related.text: The conical exterior appears as $p\to\infty$ with $\alpha p=k>1$, after scaling time and radius by $k$ [gurtug_sakalli2003].
The waves fit the cylindrical metric with two polarisations; $|\alpha p|=1$ makes the axis regular [gurtug_sakalli2003].
Xanthopoulos obtained the cylindrical waves through a complex transformation of the Kerr metric [xanthopoulos1986rotating].
The Einstein-Rosen cylindrical waves have one polarisation; the waves around the string also have a crossed polarisation [gurtug_sakalli2003].
Spinning cosmic strings carry angular momentum. The Komar angular momentum of the cylindrical wave geometry is zero [bicak_katz_lyndenbell2008].
A gravitational wave travels along a cosmic string [garfinkle1990]. Xanthopoulos's waves have cylindrical fronts around the axis [gurtug_sakalli2003].
The inverse scattering construction leads to cylindrical soliton waves around a string, with Xanthopoulos's waves in a subfamily [kleidis2010].
